title: Flaky: structural::shell_structure_light/_dark fail intermittently in parallel ui runs (theme / frame-edge global race)

labels.name: claimed
labels.description: An agent is working on this - see the claim comment

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

body:
Seen independently in two review gates on 2026-11-09 (PR #601's review, and the #330 / PR #603 work):

- `egui_app::tests::structural::shell_structure_light` failed once in a parallel `camcraft-ui --lib` run with "frame-edge sync rode the world's reference".
- `shell_structure_dark` failed once in three full runs on the dark-theme assert.
- Both pass when run alone.

**Likely cause:** a test reads or writes a process-global (the theme, or the frame-edge sync state) that another test changes concurrently.

**Expected:** structural tests are deterministic under the default parallel test runner. Either the global becomes per-harness state, or the tests that touch it are serialised.

**Done means:** the ui lib suite passes the structural tests in 20 consecutive parallel runs.

title: Viewport: Orthographic mode blanks the whole model (depth clipped by the WebGPU clip volume)

labels.name: claimed
labels.description: An agent is working on this - see the claim comment

body:
## What happens

Clicking **Orthographic** in the viewport panel (#455, shipped in v0.16.0) blanks the viewport: the model, the toolpath overlay and the stock raster all disappear, leaving only the background. Flipping back to Perspective brings everything back.

## Reproduction

In the app: open any part, click **Orthographic** beside the Shaded/Wireframe radios - the scene disappears.

Headless, on current main (`66791aa6`): the `tests/gpu_render.rs` harness, the same part as `box_stock_paints_steel_over_background`, the same `test_cam()`, only `projection` flipped:

| projection | solid pixels painted (256x256) |
| --- | --- |
| Perspective | 9,326 |
| Orthographic | 0 |

## Root cause

The ortho branch of `Camera::mvp` (`crates/ui/src/viewport.rs`, lines 1349-1350) maps depth the way OpenGL's `glOrtho` does:

```rust
m[2][2] = 2.0 / (near - far);
m[3][2] = (near + far) / (near - far);
```

which spans NDC z over [-1, +1]. WebGPU's clip volume is `-w <= x, y <= w` and `0 <= z <= w` - depth must land in [0, 1] in clip space. An ortho matrix has `clip.w == 1` (the law tests pin this), so any point with `z_ndc < 0` - every point nearer than `(near + far) / 2` - fails `0 <= z` and is clipped away before rasterization. With `near = 0.1` and `far = 40 * dist`, that midpoint is `20 * dist`, twenty times the orbit distance: everything in view is closer than the cut plane, so the whole model is clipped.

The perspective branch carries the same OpenGL-style depth row, but there `clip.w = eye_z > 0` and `z_clip` stays positive for every eye distance the camera can reach (beyond ~0.2 mm), so perspective survives - it only skews depth precision. Ortho hits the hard clip.

## Suggested fix

Map depth to [0, 1] in the ortho branch instead of [-1, +1]:

```rust
m[2][2] = 1.0 / (near - far);
m[3][2] = near / (near - far);
```

near maps to 0.0, far to 1.0, and ortho depth becomes linear. The x/y rows are already right for WebGPU. The depth attachment clears to 1.0 with `CompareFunction::Less`, so no pipeline change is needed.

## Why the tests missed it

The ortho projection law tests pin the affine row, x/y closure under orbit/zoom/dolly, and `clip.w == 1` - but nothing pins the z row, and `clip_in_front_refuses_behind_eye_points` only checks `w`. Every pixel test in `tests/gpu_render.rs` builds cameras with `..Camera::default()`, which is perspective. A law test on the ortho z span and an ortho pixel test in `gpu_render.rs` would have caught both halves.

title: Tormach post: a program leaves PathPilot in its own units (G21 stays after M30) - option to end in the machine's native units

labels.name: in-review
labels.description: Fix pushed on a branch with an open PR; merges at the next cut

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

body:
From the contributor's real-control run of #521 / PR #583 on a 770MX (2026-11-09).

**Today:** a G21 (mm) program posted for an inch-native PathPilot machine leaves the control in G21 after `M30`. In LinuxCNC, M2/M30 reset several modal groups but not units. The operator's DRO and MDI then stay in mm until they type `G20`.

**Proposal:** a post option, default off for byte-identical output, that ends the program in the machine's native unit (from the .mch unit) by writing `G20` or `G21` before `M30` when it differs from the program's unit. Alternatively, a closing comment telling the operator which units the control was left in. Check this against the LinuxCNC M2/M30 documentation, which lists what is reset.

**Done means:** with the option on, a mm program for an inch machine ends with `G20` before `M30`, and nothing changes when the units already match; with the option off, output is unchanged.

Related: #521, #583, #258 (Post dialog options).

title: Posts write the machine name into the header comment unescaped - '(' or ')' in the name breaks the program

labels.name: in-review
labels.description: Fix pushed on a branch with an open PR; merges at the next cut

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

body:
Found while building a test kit for PR #583 (2026-11-09).

**Today:**
- **What happens:** the Tormach post writes the machine's model name straight into the program's first comment. A machine named `Tormach 770MX (mm)` posted `(Tormach 770MX (mm))`.
- **Why it breaks:** LinuxCNC (PathPilot) refuses a comment nested inside a comment, so the program fails to load. Machine names come from user-editable .mch files (#478's Machines editor), so this is reachable.
- **Other posts:** they probably have the same pattern (Fanuc, Haas and Mazak write `(<machine>)` after `O0001`).

**Expected:** every text a post writes inside a comment (machine name, operation name, tool description, program comment) is sanitised to that dialect's comment-legal characters: no `(` or `)` in ISO comments, no `;` in Heidenhain, and so on. Or the name is refused when the machine file is saved.

**Done means:** a test per post with a machine and an operation whose names contain `(`/`)` posts a program whose comments parse; existing goldens are unchanged.

Related: #258 / PR #564 (program comment: it refuses `( )` at entry), #478.

title: Probe-only program: the post logs 'stock sim did not judge this program: invalid stock simulation setup' (box non-empty)

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

body:
Found while building a probe test kit for PR #583 (Tormach probing, #575), 2026-11-09.

**Today:**
- **Setup:** an inch document with a 3 × 2 × 1 in box stock equal to the part (Z -1..0), and one Probe operation (Z top-face touch). There are no cutting ops.
- **What happens:** posting succeeds but reports a non-blocking note: "stock sim did not judge this program: invalid stock simulation setup: stock box and cell must be finite, box non-empty, cell positive".
- **Why it's wrong:** the stock is finite and non-empty, so the message names the wrong cause. A probe-only program removes no stock, so the program stock sim has nothing to judge, but it should say that (or say nothing), not report an invalid setup.

**Expected:** a program with no material-removing moves either skips the stock sim with an accurate note (e.g. "no cutting moves - nothing to simulate") or runs it trivially clean. A genuinely invalid stock setup keeps its by-name refusal.

**Done means:**
- a test posts a probe-only program and gets no misleading "invalid stock simulation setup" note;
- a test with a degenerate stock still gets the real refusal.

Related: #575 / PR #583, #521.

title: Model page: a part turn or move runs no stock/part-vs-fixture interpenetration check

labels.name: in-review
labels.description: Fix pushed on a branch with an open PR; merges at the next cut

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

body:
Found in the review of PR #576 (#571).

**Today:** locate (#561, PR #566) warns by name when the part or its stock would sink into a fixture. A plain Model-page `MoveModel` (move or turn) runs no such check. Since #571 (PR #576) a turned part's square stock is refitted around it, so the regrown block could enter a vise jaw or floor with no warning. The old rigid tilt had the same gap, so this is not a regression.

**Expected:** `MoveModel` runs the same sampled part-and-stock-versus-fixture check as locate and warns by name: the moved body, the fixture and a point. A warning, not a refusal, as with locate.

**Done means:** a test moves or turns a part so its stock enters a fixture and gets the by-name warning; a clear move gets none.

title: Tool bodies: align a vendor STEP by its tool coordinate systems (ISO 13399 / GTC)

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

body:
Part of #361. Vendor tool STEP packages commonly carry named coordinate systems that place the cutting point and the mounting interface (the ISO 13399 / GTC convention). Read them when present, so a vendor body is aligned automatically instead of by hand-entered offsets. When they are absent or ambiguous, fall back to the numeric placement with a note that names why.

Sources are limited to published vendor and standard material. The coordinate-system names must be confirmed from public GTC documentation before any code; no guessing.

**Done means:** a test STEP with tool coordinate systems aligns with no manual offsets; one without them falls back by name.

title: Align the model by picking a face or two edges onto a G17/G18/G19 plane

labels.name: in-review
labels.description: Fix pushed on a branch with an open PR; merges at the next cut

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

body:
Requested by the maintainer (2026-11-08), part of the setup/orientation problem: "a Face or two edges should be possible to locate to a G17-G19 plane as a shortcut to the turn and tilt offset functions - this is on the model."

## What
A one-click way to orient the **model** (not the work offset) by picking geometry:

- **Pick a planar face** -> choose a target plane: **G17 (XY)**, **G18 (ZX)** or **G19 (YZ)**. The model is rotated so that face lies on/parallel to the chosen plane, its outward normal along the plane's axis (+Z for G17, +Y for G18, +X for G19; a "flip" toggle for the opposite direction).
- **Pick two edges** (two non-parallel linear edges, or two coplanar edges) -> they define a plane the same way, and the first edge also fixes the rotation about the plane normal (it is laid along the plane's first axis: X for G17/G18, Y for G19).
- Optionally, place the result: snap the picked face onto the plane's level (e.g. face to Z=0) or keep the model's current position.

It is a shortcut for the existing turn/tilt (rotate model) functions: the same rotation, computed from the pick instead of typed angles.

## Where it fits
- It acts on the **model orientation** - the part's alignment. With #326 (per-setup part alignment to the setup's frame) it should write that setup's part alignment (so a second setup can lay a different face down); until #326 lands, it uses the document-level model transform (`MoveModel`).
- It does **not** rotate the work offset (that path is #187's 3-2-1, now refused when rotated by #315/PR #325) - program zero stays a plain translation (#196 / PR #328).

## Rules
- One undoable command (the same command the rotate/tilt functions use, with the computed rotation), written on command creation.
- Refuse by name: a non-planar face; two parallel or coincident edges, or a curved edge; a degenerate face; a pick on something that is not the model.
- Stock and toolpaths react as they do to a manual rotate today (stock re-fits if it is fitted to the model; operations go stale).

## Done means
Face -> G17/G18/G19 and two edges -> G17/G18/G19 both orient the model exactly (normal within a tight angular tolerance of the target axis; edge along the target axis), undo restores the previous orientation, the refusals fire by name, pinned by app tests (rotation math on known faces/edges of a fixture block and a tilted fixture) and a UI test of the pick flow.

Related: #326 (per-setup part alignment), #316 (transform between setups), #187 (3-2-1 work offset align), #315, #196 / PR #328, #308.
